title: Mastering Incomitant Strabismus: Paralytic vs. Restrictive
summary: Incomitant strabismus presents a diagnostic challenge where the angle of deviation varies with the direction of gaze. Differentiating between neurogenic paralysis and mechanical restriction is crucial for appropriate surgical and medical management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Incomitant strabismus is a misalignment of the visual axes where the angle of deviation changes by more than 5 prism diopters (PD) in different positions of gaze. It is broadly categorized into Paralytic (failure of innervation) and Restrictive (mechanical tethering or physical obstruction of movement).

sections.title: The Core Laws of Ocular Motility

branches: Hering's Law: Equal/simultaneous innervation to yoke muscles
Sherrington's Law: Increased innervation to agonist = decreased to antagonist
Donder's Law: Eye position determines orientation regardless of path taken

rows: Overaction of yoke; contracture of antagonist

sections.title: Step-by-Step: Forced Duction Test (FDT)
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine or 4% Cocaine) or subconjunctival Lidocaine.
Step 2: Grasp the conjunctiva/Tenon's capsule at the limbus with 0.5 toothed forceps opposite the direction of limited movement.
Step 3: Attempt to passively move the globe into the restricted field of gaze.
Step 4: If resistance is felt, the test is POSITIVE (Restrictive). If the eye moves freely, it is NEGATIVE (Paralytic).
Step 5: Perform Forced Generation Test (FGT) to assess active muscle force (palsy vs. restriction).

sections.title: Neurological Red Flags
content: CN III Palsy with Pupil Involvement (Rule out PCOM Aneurysm!)
Sudden onset diplopia with severe headache (GCA or Hemorrhage)
Bilateral CN VI Palsy (Increased Intracranial Pressure)
Proptosis with restricted motility (Orbital Cellulitis or Apex Mass)
Diurnal variation/Fatigability (Myasthenia Gravis Crisis risk)

sections.title: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test (Vertical Diplopia)
content: 1. Identify which eye is Hypertropic in Primary Gaze.
2. Determine if Hypertropia increases in Right or Left Gaze.
3. Determine if Hypertropia increases on Right or Left Head Tilt.
Clinical Goal: To isolate a paretic vertical muscle (usually the Superior Oblique).

content.explanation: Order of muscle involvement in Thyroid Eye Disease: Inferior Rectus > Medial Rectus > Superior Rectus > Lateral Rectus.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Essentials
content: Hess Screen or Lancaster Red-Green Test: Quantifies incomitancy.
Prism Under Cover Test (PUCT): Measured in 9 cardinal positions.
Orbit/Brain MRI/MRA: Essential for non-vasculopathic CN palsies or TED.
Blood Work: HbA1c, BP, TFTs (TSH/T3/T4), Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies.
Ice Pack/Tensilon Test: For suspected Myasthenia Gravis.
Saccadic Velocity assessment (Clinical observation or EOG).

sections.title: Surgical Management Principles
content: Paralytic: Strengthen the paretic muscle (Resection) or Weaken the overacting antagonist (Recession).
Paralytic (Total): Transposition procedures (e.g., Knapp, Hummelsheim, Nishida).
Restrictive: Recess the restricted muscle. DO NOT resect a restricted muscle.
Botulinum Toxin: Useful in acute CN VI palsy to prevent medial rectus contracture.
Adjustable Sutures: Highly recommended in incomitant/restrictive cases.

rows: Agenesis of CN VI nuclei; LR innervated by CN III
Limited Abduction + Globe retraction on Adduction
Inability to elevate in Adduction; 'Click' sound
Congenital CN VI and VII palsy
Entrapment of IR in maxillary sinus

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Primary Deviation: Normal eye fixing, paretic eye deviating. Secondary Deviation: Paretic eye fixing, normal eye deviating. Secondary is always larger in paralysis due to Hering's Law.
In CN IV palsy, the head tilts AWAY from the side of the lesion to minimize the vertical and torsional component.
Pseudo-Von Graefe sign (lid dyskinesia) is a hallmark of aberrant regeneration in CN III palsy.
In TED, the IR is most commonly affected, leading to a restrictive hypotropia (limitation of elevation).
Saccadic 'Floating' suggests paralysis; 'Abrupt Stop' suggests restriction.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Data
sections.content: The IRIS registry highlights that microvascular CN palsies have a >70% spontaneous recovery rate within 6 months. Recent surgical advances include 'Plication' as a safer alternative to Resection to preserve anterior segment ischemia, especially in elderly patients with multiple muscle surgeries.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Risk of Anterior Segment Ischemia (ASI) if >2 rectus muscles are operated on simultaneously.
Recurrence of restriction in TED if thyroid status is not stabilized.
Permanent diplopia if sensory fusion is lost (rare in adults).
Consecutive deviations following over-correction.
